Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Idealized Families: Happy families, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mai was thirty-eight years old, a stock broker who had spent fifteen years in a profession that rewarded the ability to stay calm under pressure, to read a room of screaming traders and make split-second decisions while the noise rose around her. She had been good at that, once. She had thrived on the chaos of the open floor, the adrenaline of a volatile market, the way her mind could cut through the roar and find the signal. That was before the stalking, before she understood that noise could mean something entirely different.

The stalking had lasted eight months, though Mai still could not say with certainty when it had truly begun. It had started with small things—a car that seemed to linger near her apartment building, a text from an unknown number that read only with her name. She had dismissed it, told herself she was being paranoid, that the city was full of people and coincidences happened. But the man had been methodical. He had learned her schedule, her route to work, the coffee shop she visited every Tuesday morning. He had left a single rose on her desk once, in the middle of the night, and Mai had not slept for three days afterward. The police had been polite but useless. No direct threats, they said. No physical contact. They could not do anything until he did something, and Mai had spent those months waiting for him to do something, certain that he would.

The night it ended, he had been waiting in the stairwell of her building. He had not touched her. He had simply stood there, blocking the door to her floor, and smiled. Mai had frozen. She remembered the smell of alcohol on his breath, sour and sharp, and the way the fluorescent light had flickered above them. She had turned and run, down three flights of stairs, out into the street, and she had not stopped running until she reached a twenty-four-hour diner six blocks away. She had called her partner from there, her hands shaking so badly she could barely press the buttons. The man had been arrested two days later, after a neighbor reported someone loitering in the stairwell again, and Mai had thought that would be the end of it.

It was not the end of it. The memory of that night did not feel like a memory. When Mai thought about the stairwell, she did not remember it the way she remembered other things—flat and distant, like a photograph in an album. She felt it. The cold of the concrete through her shoes. The flicker of the light. The smell. The smile. Her heart would begin to pound, her palms would sweat, and she would lose track of where she was. She would be back there, standing in front of him, and the terror was not a recollection—it was present, alive, as real as the moment it had happened. Sometimes, in the middle of a quiet evening at home, she would catch a whiff of something—a neighbor cooking, a passerby drinking from a flask—and her body would react before her mind could catch up. Her breath would catch. Her shoulders would tense. She would scan the room for exits, for faces, for anything that might be a threat.

The noise was the hardest part. The trading floor had become unbearable. Every shout, every slammed phone, every sudden burst of laughter sent a jolt through her chest. She had taken to wearing noise-canceling headphones, but that only isolated her, made her seem distant and unapproachable to colleagues who had once relied on her quick reads and steady hand. Her performance had slipped. She had missed a major trade last quarter because she had frozen—a loud crash from the break room had sent her into the stairwell again, and by the time she had come back to herself, the opportunity was gone. Her supervisor had pulled her aside, asked if everything was all right. Mai had said yes, because what else could she say? That she could not trust her own mind? That the memory of a man standing in a stairwell had cost her thirty thousand dollars?

She had changed her route to work three times. She avoided the coffee shop. She crossed the street whenever she saw a family—a mother and father with children, laughing, ordinary—because something about their happiness felt like a lie, like the world was pretending to be safe when she knew it was not. She had stopped going out to bars with her colleagues. The smell of alcohol, even from across a room, could send her spiraling. Her partner had been patient, but Mai could see the strain. They had not gone on a date in months. They did not talk about it. Mai did not know how to explain that the worst part was not the fear itself, but the way the memory refused to stay in the past. It was still happening. That was what she could not shake. It was still happening, and she was still in the stairwell, and no one could convince her otherwise.

She had come to therapy because her partner had finally said, gently, that she seemed like she was drowning. Mai had not argued. She had filled out the questionnaire in the waiting room, circling numbers that added up to something she did not want to name. She sat now in the therapist’s office, her hands folded in her lap, and she said, “I don’t know how to make it stop feeling real.” She was not sure if she was asking for help or simply stating a fact. She was afraid that the answer was the same either way.
